items.headline: FinCEN orders US financial institutions to stop transfers involving MEXC Global
items.what_happened: On 6 November 2026, FinCEN announced an order under section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act prohibiting US financial institutions from transmitting funds to or from MEXC Global. Treasury says the virtual asset exchanger facilitated at least USD 16 billion in transactions connected to sanctions evasion, cybercrime and other illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026. Treasury states the order becomes effective 30 days after Federal Register publication.
items.why_it_matters: The USD 16 billion is Treasury and FinCEN’s attributed transaction figure, not a court judgment or a customer loss calculation. The order is a specific US funds transfer prohibition and does not itself impose a worldwide ban on every user of the platform. Its effective date must be calculated from the actual Federal Register publication, not the press release date.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. US exposed institutions should inventory direct and indirect MEXC payment pathways, distinguish section 9714 restrictions from OFAC blocking obligations, confirm the Federal Register effective date and record disposition of attempted transfers. Other institutions should assess applicable local law and correspondent exposure rather than assume US rules apply universally.

items.headline: FATF maps financial flows supporting transnational scam compounds
items.what_happened: On 5 November 2026, FATF published a report on illicit financial flows linked to scam compounds. It describes interconnected fraud, human trafficking and laundering operations and the use of money mule accounts, cash, informal transfer services and virtual assets. FATF reports that people from at least 80 jurisdictions have been identified in Southeast Asian scam compounds and cites an estimate of 120,000 people forced to carry out online scams in Myanmar alone.
items.why_it_matters: The report identifies two different victim groups: people coerced into conducting scams and people defrauded by them. The numerical estimates and illustrative blockchain tracing examples must not be recast as verified totals for all global fraud losses. Monitoring only the final cash out misses earlier infrastructure and payment routing signals.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Link scam investigation signals across recruitment, receiving accounts, rapid onward transfers, crypto conversion and common counterparties. Keep hypotheses about coerced workers separate from evidence of knowing participation, and record attribution and confidence for wallet cluster or network linkages.

items.headline: OFAC targets corporate infrastructure supporting Prince Group scam operations
items.what_happened: On 5 November 2026, OFAC announced designations of four individuals and 41 entities supporting the Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization business network, plus one Malaysian individual associated with an Africa based scam network. Treasury describes offshore holdings, nominee arrangements, property transfers and professional facilitators supporting access to financial systems following earlier designations.
items.why_it_matters: The action targets ownership and facilitation structures rather than only the alleged operators of scams. The release describes 46 targets in total, with distinct designation authorities. An OFAC designation is a legal sanctions action, while underlying conduct descriptions are Treasury findings and allegations, not interchangeable with criminal convictions.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Screen newly designated parties and test direct and indirect ownership, including OFAC’s aggregate 50 percent rule where applicable. Investigate beneficial ownership changes and transfers involving previously designated principals, preserving evidence and distinguishing confirmed matches from associative leads.

items.headline: OFAC designates eight Canadian money services businesses over Iran related crypto activity
items.what_happened: On 6 November 2026, OFAC designated eight Canada based money services businesses under Executive Order 13902. Treasury says the firms facilitated transactions involving Iranian currencies and digital assets, including activity linked to sanctioned Iranian exchanges and IRGC associated addresses. Treasury describes overlapping exposure to drug proceeds in some cases and coordination with FINTRAC.
items.why_it_matters: These are US designations of specified businesses, not a determination that all Canadian MSBs or Iran related remittances are illicit. Trade names, corporate legal names, digital asset addresses and changes in business identity may complicate screening. Treasury’s characterisation of transactions should be attributed to Treasury.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Update relevant OFAC data, map legal names to trading names, and review wallet and payment exposures with confidence graded attribution. Check applicable US nexus, blocking, reporting and ownership rules; do not automatically infer Canadian or UK designation from the US action.

items.headline: US Treasury targets false flagging and certification network serving Iran shadow fleet
items.what_happened: On 4 November 2026, US Treasury announced sanctions against a maritime network it says supplied false vessel flags and certifications to ships transporting Iranian petroleum. Treasury identified India based Suniel Kumar Sharma and Jaspreet Preeti Shahid and described purported flagging and classification arrangements across jurisdictions. OFAC also announced an industry alert on the sanctions risks of potentially falsely flagged vessels.
items.why_it_matters: Vessel identity risk is not resolved by matching the ship name alone. Flag state claims, registry authority, classification documents, IMO numbers, insurers and ownership structures can diverge. The release contains Treasury’s allegations and designations; it is not proof that every vessel bearing a particular flag is illicit.
items.radar_implication: This is FinCrimeRadar analysis. Validate vessel identifiers and certificates against authoritative flag and classification sources, retain dated evidence, and escalate conflicting registration or insurance records. Apply sanctions controls to confirmed parties and transactions under the relevant jurisdiction rather than treating a documentation anomaly as a conclusive sanctions match.
